subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 71-year-old man with a long history of heavy tobacco use presents with lightheadedness and vertigo that reliably develop after several minutes of raking leaves with his left arm. He reports left arm pain and paresthesias with exertion. His left radial pulse is weak and delayed compared with the right. Systolic blood pressure is 168 mm Hg in the right arm and 142 mm Hg in the left arm.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's neurologic symptoms?

options.text: Reversed blood flow in the right vertebral artery
Microembolization of cholesterol debris from an aortic arch plaque into the cerebral circulation
Compression of the subclavian artery by an accessory cervical rib
Reduced perfusion of both arms and the brain from a juxtaductal aortic narrowing
Stenosis of the left subclavian artery proximal to the vertebral artery origin, causing reversed blood flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery and reduced cerebral perfusion during left arm exertion

explanation_correct: Subclavian steal syndrome occurs when stenosis of the subclavian artery proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery causes hypoperfusion distal to the stenosis; blood is then stolen by reversed flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery during arm exertion, reducing cerebral perfusion. This produces arm ischemia with pain and paresthesias plus vertebrobasilar insufficiency (dizziness, vertigo) and a systolic blood pressure difference >15 mm Hg between arms — here 26 mm Hg.

explanation_incorrect.A: Flow reversal occurs in the ipsilateral (left) vertebral artery, distal to the stenosed segment; the right vertebral artery is unaffected because the right subclavian is not stenosed.
explanation_incorrect.B: Cholesterol microembolization causes livedo reticularis, blue toes, and organ ischemia after vascular procedures, and does not produce symptoms selectively with left arm exertion.
explanation_incorrect.C: External compression by a cervical rib describes thoracic outlet syndrome, which causes arm symptoms without reversed vertebral flow or cerebral hypoperfusion on exertion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Juxtaductal aortic narrowing (coarctation) causes upper-extremity hypertension and weak, delayed lower-extremity pulses, not a >15 mm Hg difference between the two arms with exertional vertigo.

educationalObjective: Explain subclavian steal syndrome: proximal subclavian stenosis with reversed ipsilateral vertebral flow causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency on arm exertion.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 66-year-old woman with hypertension and hyperlipidemia is found during a routine visit to have a 24 mm Hg difference in systolic blood pressure between her right and left arms. On questioning, she describes dizziness after carrying heavy bags with her left arm. Duplex ultrasonography demonstrates reversed flow in the left vertebral artery.
question: Which of the following is the most common cause of this syndrome?
explanation_correct: A >15 mm Hg systolic blood pressure difference between arms, vertebrobasilar symptoms on arm exertion, and reversed ipsilateral vertebral flow identify subclavian steal syndrome. The most common cause is atherosclerosis of the subclavian artery proximal to the vertebral artery origin. Takayasu arteritis and heart surgery are other recognized associations, but atherosclerosis is by far the most common in older patients with this woman's risk profile.

explanation_incorrect.A: Takayasu arteritis is an associated cause of subclavian stenosis, classically in young women, but it is not the most common cause; atherosclerosis is.
explanation_incorrect.C: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis affects branches of the external carotid artery and is not a recognized cause of subclavian steal syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Radiation therapy can stenose arteries but is not listed among the common causes; it is not the most common cause of the syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Thromboangiitis obliterans is a distal, inflammatory, thrombotic disease of young heavy smokers affecting the extremities, not a proximal subclavian stenosis syndrome.

educationalObjective: Recall that atherosclerosis is the most common cause of subclavian steal syndrome (other associations: Takayasu arteritis, heart surgery).
